title: Advanced idioms: heart, hand, head and eye
titleFa: اصطلاحات دل و دست و سر و چشم
titleR: estelāhāt-e del o dast o sar o cheshm
intro: Persian feels with the heart and the liver, works with the hands and feet, and judges with the head, eyes, face, ears and tongue. Iranians use body idioms all day long – to say they miss you, that they doubt something, that someone conned them or that they are too shy to ask. This lesson teaches 30 of the most useful, each with its literal picture, its meaning, its register and an example, and a long conversation where they come thick and fast.
goals: understand and use 30 everyday idioms built on دل، جگر، دست، پا، سر، چشم، رو، گوش and زبان
picture the literal image behind each idiom and remember it through that image
attach the possessive ending to the body part, not the verb: دلم تنگ شده
choose an idiom that fits the register – affectionate, everyday, informal or literary

sections.title: A letter from home
sections.intro: Leila writes to her brother Dariush, who has been studying in Germany for two years. Family news in Persian is hard to tell without body idioms – count how many you find.

sentences.fa: نمی‌دانی چقدر دلمان برایت تنگ شده است.
sentences.r: nemi-dāni cheghadr del-emān barā-yat tang shode ast.
sentences.en: You can't imagine how much we miss you.
sentences.lit: you don't know how much our heart has become tight for you

sentences.fa: مامان هر شب گوش به زنگ است که زنگ بزنی.
sentences.r: Māmān har shab gush be zang ast ke zang bezani.
sentences.en: Every evening Mum is on the alert, waiting for you to call.

sentences.fa: هفته‌ی پیش عکست را دید که لاغر شده‌ای و جگرش کباب شد.
sentences.r: hafte-ye pish aks-at rā did ke lāghar shode-i o jegar-ash kabāb shod.
sentences.en: Last week she saw in your photo that you've got thin, and her heart bled for you.

sentences.fa: من هم سرم خیلی شلوغ است، ولی هر روز به یادت هستم.
sentences.r: man ham sar-am kheyli sholugh ast, vali har ruz be yād-at hastam.
sentences.en: I'm swamped too, but I think of you every day.

sentences.fa: خبر بزرگ این است که مهسا آخر دلش را به دریا زد و کافه‌اش را باز کرد.
sentences.r: khabar-e bozorg in ast ke Mahsā ākhar del-ash rā be daryā zad o kāfe-ash rā bāz kard.
sentences.en: The big news is that Mahsa finally took the plunge and opened her café.
sentences.lit: she threw her heart into the sea

sentences.fa: ماه‌ها دل‌دل می‌کرد، اما حالا پشیمان نیست.
sentences.r: māh-hā del-del mi-kard, ammā hālā pashimān nist.
sentences.en: She dithered for months, but now she has no regrets.

sentences.fa: من و امیر هم پا به پایش کار کردیم تا مغازه آماده شد.
sentences.r: man o Amir ham pā be pā-yash kār kardim tā maghāze āmāde shod.
sentences.en: Amir and I worked alongside her, step for step, until the place was ready.

sentences.fa: بابا اول گفت چشمش آب نمی‌خورد که این کار بگیرد.
sentences.r: Bābā avval goft cheshm-ash āb nemi-khorad ke in kār begirad.
sentences.en: At first Dad said he doubted the business would take off.

sentences.fa: ولی حالا هر روز آن‌جا می‌نشیند و با مشتری‌ها سر به سر می‌گذارد.
sentences.r: vali hālā har ruz ān-jā mi-neshinad o bā moshtari-hā sar be sar mi-gozārad.
sentences.en: But now he sits there every day and teases the customers.

sentences.fa: یکی از همسایه‌ها می‌خواست سر مهسا کلاه بگذارد و اجاره را دو برابر کند.
sentences.r: yek-i az hamsāye-hā mi-khāst sar-e Mahsā kolāh begozārad o ejāre rā do barābar konad.
sentences.en: One of the neighbours tried to con Mahsa and double the rent.
sentences.lit: to put a hat on Mahsa's head

sentences.fa: اما وکیلمان دستش را رو کرد و او دیگر جرئت نکرد.
sentences.r: ammā vakil-emān dast-ash rā ru kard o u digar jor'at na-kard.
sentences.en: But our lawyer exposed his game, and he didn't dare try again.

sentences.fa: مامان می‌گوید زیادی به او رو داده بودیم.
sentences.r: Māmān mi-guyad ziyādi be u ru dāde budim.
sentences.en: Mum says we had given him far too much leeway.

sentences.fa: من زبان به دهان گرفتم و چیزی نگفتم، چون نمی‌خواستم دل کسی را بشکنم.
sentences.r: man zabān be dahān gereftam o chiz-i na-goftam, chon nemi-khāstam del-e kas-i rā beshkanam.
sentences.en: I held my tongue and said nothing, because I didn't want to hurt anyone's feelings.

sentences.fa: زود بیا که همه چشم به راهت هستیم.
sentences.r: zud biyā ke hame cheshm be rāh-at hastim.
sentences.en: Come home soon – we're all waiting for you.

sections.title: Your body is a dictionary
sections.md:
Most Persian body idioms are **compound verbs**: a body part plus a common verb – شدن، کردن، دادن، گذاشتن، زدن، گرفتن. Three things make them work.

**1. The body part is often the grammatical subject.** In [[دلم تنگ شده|del-am tang shode|I miss (it/you)]] the subject is 'my heart', not 'I'. So the possessive ending goes on the body part and the verb stays in the third person singular: *del-am tang shode*, *del-et tang shode*, *del-esh tang shode* – never *del tang shode-am*.

**2. Another person enters with the ezafe or a preposition.** [[سر کسی کلاه گذاشتن|sar-e kas-i kolāh gozāshtan]] – put a hat on *someone's* head; [[دلم برایت تنگ شده|del-am barā-yat tang shode]] – my heart is tight *for you*.

**3. The literal picture is your memory aid.** A tight heart is a homesick heart; an eye that 'drinks no water' doubts; a liver roasted like kebab is grief for someone else's pain. In older Persian the **liver** (جگر) was a seat of feeling as much as the heart, which is why it turns up in the most emotional idioms.

Register matters. Some idioms are **affectionate** (جگرگوشه), many are **everyday** (سرم شلوغ است), some are **informal** – fine with friends, too familiar for a job interview (سر کسی کلاه گذاشتن) – and a few sound **literary** (زبان به دهان گرفتن). The tables give a register for each.

items.lit: my heart has become tight for you
items.note: everyday, affectionate; spoken: دلم برات تنگ شده (del-am barāt tang shode)

ex.fa: دلم برای غذای مادرم تنگ شده است.
ex.r: del-am barā-ye ghazā-ye mādar-am tang shode ast.
ex.en: I miss my mother's cooking.
ex.col: دلم واسه غذای مامانم تنگ شده.
ex.colR: del-am vāse ghazā-ye māmān-am tang shode.

items.en: I feel down, I'm in low spirits
items.lit: my heart has been seized

ex.fa: امروز هوا ابری است و دلم گرفته.
ex.r: emruz havā abri ast o del-am gerefte.
ex.en: It's cloudy today and I feel low.

items.en: to take something to heart, be hurt by it
items.lit: to take into the heart
items.note: everyday; very common in the negative imperative

ex.fa: شوخی کردم؛ به دل نگیر.
ex.r: shukhi kardam; be del na-gir.
ex.en: I was joking – don't take it to heart.

items.lit: to break someone's heart
items.note: neutral; weaker than English 'break someone's heart'

ex.fa: با یک حرف ساده دلش را شکستی.
ex.r: bā yek harf-e sāde del-ash rā shekasti.
ex.en: You hurt her feelings with one careless word.

items.en: to take the plunge, risk it
items.lit: to throw one's heart into the sea

ex.fa: دلم را به دریا زدم و استعفا دادم.
ex.r: del-am rā be daryā zadam o este'fā dādam.
ex.en: I took the plunge and resigned.

items.lit: my heart burned for his state

ex.fa: وقتی دیدمش، دلم به حالش سوخت.
ex.r: vaghti didam-ash, del-am be hāl-ash sukht.
ex.en: When I saw him, I felt sorry for him.

items.en: my heart bled (for someone), I was heartbroken
items.lit: my liver was roasted like kebab
items.note: emotional, everyday; for pity and grief, not romance

ex.fa: جگرم کباب شد وقتی خبر زلزله را شنیدم.
ex.r: jegar-am kabāb shod vaghti khabar-e zelzele rā shenidam.
ex.en: My heart bled when I heard the news of the earthquake.

items.en: to expose someone's game or trick
items.lit: to turn someone's hand face up (like cards)
items.note: informal; passive: دستش رو شد 'his game was up'

ex.fa: دستش رو شد؛ همه فهمیدند دروغ می‌گفت.
ex.r: dast-ash ru shod; hame fahmidand dorugh mi-goft.
ex.en: His game was up – everyone realised he had been lying.

items.lit: to give hand to each other's hand

ex.fa: همسایه‌ها دست به دست هم دادند و کوچه را تمیز کردند.
ex.r: hamsāye-hā dast be dast-e ham dādand o kuche rā tamiz kardand.
ex.en: The neighbours joined forces and cleaned up the street.

items.fa: کسی را دست به سر کردن
items.r: kas-i rā dast be sar kardan
items.en: to fob someone off, get rid of someone with excuses
items.lit: to put a hand to someone's head

ex.fa: هر بار می‌پرسم، مرا با یک بهانه دست به سر می‌کند.
ex.r: har bār mi-porsam, marā bā yek bahāne dast be sar mi-konad.
ex.en: Every time I ask, he fobs me off with an excuse.
ex.col: هر دفعه می‌پرسم، منو با یه بهونه دست به سر می‌کنه.
ex.colR: har daf'e mi-porsam, mano bā ye bahune dast be sar mi-kone.

items.lit: to lift one's hand off someone's head
items.note: informal; دست از سرم بردار! can be rude

ex.fa: دست از سرم بردار؛ کار دارم!
ex.r: dast az sar-am bardār; kār dāram!
ex.en: Leave me alone – I'm busy!

items.en: alongside someone, keeping pace with them
items.lit: foot to someone's foot

ex.fa: پدرم در همه‌ی سختی‌ها پا به پای ما آمد.
ex.r: pedar-am dar hame-ye sakhti-hā pā be pā-ye mā āmad.
ex.en: My father stood by us through all the hard times.

items.lit: to stand at the foot of one's words

ex.fa: او پای حرفش ایستاد و پول را پس داد.
ex.r: u pā-ye harf-ash istād o pul rā pas dād.
ex.en: He kept his word and paid the money back.

items.lit: to put head to someone's head

ex.fa: داری سر به سرم می‌گذاری؟
ex.r: dāri sar be sar-am mi-gozāri?
ex.en: Are you teasing me?

items.lit: my head is crowded

ex.fa: این هفته سرم خیلی شلوغ است.
ex.r: in hafte sar-am kheyli sholugh ast.
ex.en: I'm really busy this week.

items.lit: to put a hat on someone's head

ex.fa: فروشنده سرمان کلاه گذاشت؛ این گوشی دست‌دوم بود.
ex.r: forushande sar-emān kolāh gozāsht; in gushi dast-e-dovvom bud.
ex.en: The seller conned us – this phone was second-hand.

items.en: I doubt it, I don't believe it will happen
items.lit: my eye doesn't drink water

ex.fa: چشمم آب نمی‌خورد که او سر وقت بیاید.
ex.r: cheshm-am āb nemi-khorad ke u sar-e vaght biyāyad.
ex.en: I doubt he'll come on time.

items.lit: to have one's eye on the road

ex.fa: خانواده‌اش سال‌ها چشم به راه او بودند.
ex.r: khānevāde-ash sāl-hā cheshm be rāh-e u budand.
ex.en: His family waited for him for years.

items.en: congratulations (on a new baby, a return, good news)
items.lit: may your eye be bright
items.note: everyday; also ironic: 'well, isn't that great!'

ex.fa: چشمت روشن! شنیدم نوه‌دار شدی.
ex.r: cheshm-at roshan! shenidam nave-dār shodi.
ex.en: Congratulations! I hear you've become a grandmother.

items.en: to give someone too much leeway, spoil them
items.lit: to give face

ex.fa: زیادی به بچه‌ها رو می‌دهی.
ex.r: ziyādi be bacche-hā ru mi-dahi.
ex.en: You let the children get away with too much.

items.lit: my face doesn't become (able)

ex.fa: رویم نمی‌شود دوباره از او پول قرض بگیرم.
ex.r: ru-yam nemi-shavad dobāre az u pul gharz begiram.
ex.en: I'm too embarrassed to borrow money from him again.
ex.col: روم نمی‌شه دوباره ازش پول قرض بگیرم.
ex.colR: ru-m nemi-she dobāre az-ash pul gharz begiram.

items.en: to be on the alert, waiting for news
items.lit: to have one's ear to the bell

ex.fa: منتظر نتیجه‌ی آزمایش هستم و گوش به زنگم.
ex.r: montazer-e natije-ye āzmāyesh hastam o gush be zang-am.
ex.en: I'm waiting for the test results and on the alert.

items.lit: his ear is not in debt

ex.fa: گوشش بدهکار نیست؛ هر چه می‌گویم کار خودش را می‌کند.
ex.r: gush-ash bedehkār nist; har che mi-guyam kār-e khod-ash rā mi-konad.
ex.en: He won't listen – whatever I say, he does as he pleases.

items.lit: to take one's tongue into one's mouth
items.note: neutral to literary; زبان به دهان بگیر! 'hold your tongue!' is sharp

ex.fa: بهتر است فعلاً زبان به دهان بگیری.
ex.r: behtar ast fe'lan zabān be dahān begiri.
ex.en: You'd better keep quiet for now.

sections.title: Heart and liver: feelings
sections.md:
With [[دل|del]] the person who feels is shown by the **possessive ending on دل**, and the verb stays third person singular: [[دلم گرفت|del-am gereft|I felt low]], [[دلت گرفت|del-et gereft|you felt low]], [[دلشان گرفت|del-eshān gereft|they felt low]]. The thing or person you feel for comes with [[برای|barā-ye]] or [[به حال|be hāl-e]].

[[جگر|jegar|liver]] belongs to the strongest feelings: compassion, grief, and the love of parents for children. Iranians also say [[جیگر|jigar]] in slang to mean 'darling' or 'gorgeous' – affectionate between friends and family, but too familiar to say to strangers.

sections.title: Hands and feet: action and loyalty
sections.md:
[[دست|dast|hand]] idioms are about doing – helping, cheating, giving up, being generous. [[پا|pā|foot]] idioms are about standing somewhere: beside a friend, between two people who have quarrelled, behind your own word.

Notice the small words. **به** joins two body parts: [[دست به دست|dast be dast|hand to hand]], [[پا به پا|pā be pā|foot to foot]]. **از** means 'off': [[دست از سر کسی برداشتن|dast az sar-e kas-i bardāshtan|to take one's hand off someone's head]]. And in [[دستش رو شد|dast-ash ru shod|his game was up]] the active رو کردن becomes رو شدن, just as کردن becomes شدن in any passive.

sections.title: Head, eyes, face, ears and tongue
sections.md:
The head ([[سر|sar]]) thinks, gets busy and gets tricked; the eye ([[چشم|cheshm]]) waits, doubts and rejoices; the face ([[رو|ru]]) is your honour and your shyness; the ear ([[گوش|gush]]) listens or refuses to; the tongue ([[زبان|zabān]]) is best kept still.

Two patterns are worth noticing. With **رو** the idea is *face* as in 'losing face': [[رویم نمی‌شود|ru-yam nemi-shavad]] is 'my face can't manage it' – I'm too embarrassed. With **چشم** many idioms are blessings: [[چشمت روشن|cheshm-at roshan]] 'may your eyes be bright' is what you say to someone whose son has come home or whose grandchild has just been born.

examples.fa: چشم‌وهم‌چشمی باعث شد عروسی‌شان آن‌قدر گران شود.
examples.r: cheshm-o-ham-cheshmi bā'es shod arusi-shān ān-ghadr gerān shavad.
examples.en: Keeping up with the neighbours made their wedding so expensive.

examples.fa: بچه‌ها، سر به سر مادربزرگ نگذارید!
examples.r: bacche-hā, sar be sar-e mādar-bozorg na-gozārid!
examples.en: Children, don't tease Grandma!
examples.col: بچه‌ها، سر به سر مادربزرگ نذارین!
examples.colR: bacche-hā, sar be sar-e mādar-bozorg na-zārin!

examples.fa: چشمت روشن! پسرت سرانجام از سفر برگشت.
examples.r: cheshm-at roshan! pesar-at saranjām az safar bargasht.
examples.en: Congratulations! Your son is home from his travels at last.

examples.fa: گوشم بدهکار نیست؛ تا عذرخواهی نکنی، نمی‌بخشمت.
examples.r: gush-am bedehkār nist; tā ozr-khāhi na-koni, nemi-bakhsham-at.
examples.en: I'm not listening – until you apologise, I won't forgive you.

examples.fa: در جلسه زبان به دهان گرفتم، ولی بعد همه چیز را به مدیر گفتم.
examples.r: dar jalase zabān be dahān gereftam, vali ba'd hame chiz rā be modir goftam.
examples.en: In the meeting I held my tongue, but afterwards I told the manager everything.

examples.fa: شب امتحان همه گوش به زنگ بودند که نتیجه‌ها اعلام شود.
examples.r: shab-e emtehān hame gush be zang budand ke natije-hā e'lām shavad.
examples.en: The night of the exam, everyone was on the alert for the results to be announced.

examples.fa: رویش نشد بگوید که پول ندارد.
examples.r: ru-yash na-shod beguyad ke pul na-dārad.
examples.en: He was too embarrassed to say he had no money.

sections.title: The report that never comes
sections.context: Sara and Amir work in the same office. Their colleague Reza promised to finish a report days ago. Listen for the idioms – there are more than a dozen.

lines.fa: سارا، رضا گزارش را تمام کرد؟
lines.r: Sārā, Rezā gozāresh rā tamām kard?
lines.en: Sara, did Reza finish the report?

lines.fa: نه! سه روز است مرا دست به سر می‌کند: «فردا، فردا».
lines.r: na! se ruz ast marā dast be sar mi-konad: «fardā, fardā».
lines.en: No! For three days he's been fobbing me off: 'Tomorrow, tomorrow.'
lines.col: نه! سه روزه منو دست به سر می‌کنه: «فردا، فردا».
lines.colR: na! se ruz-e mano dast be sar mi-kone: «fardā, fardā».

lines.fa: چشمم آب نمی‌خورد که تا پنجشنبه تمامش کند.
lines.r: cheshm-am āb nemi-khorad ke tā panjshanbe tamām-ash konad.
lines.en: I doubt he'll finish it by Thursday.
lines.col: چشمم آب نمی‌خوره تا پنجشنبه تمومش کنه.
lines.colR: cheshm-am āb nemi-khore tā panjshanbe tamum-esh kone.

lines.fa: تقصیر خودمان است؛ زیادی به او رو دادیم.
lines.r: taghsir-e khod-emān ast; ziyādi be u ru dādim.
lines.en: It's our own fault – we've given him far too much leeway.
lines.col: تقصیر خودمونه؛ زیادی بهش رو دادیم.
lines.colR: taghsir-e khod-emun-e; ziyādi beh-esh ru dādim.

lines.fa: بیا دست به دست هم بدهیم و خودمان تمامش کنیم.
lines.r: biyā dast be dast-e ham bedahim o khod-emān tamām-ash konim.
lines.en: Let's join forces and finish it ourselves.
lines.col: بیا دست به دست هم بدیم، خودمون تمومش کنیم.
lines.colR: biyā dast be dast-e ham bedim, khod-emun tamum-esh konim.

lines.fa: باشد، ولی رویم نمی‌شود به خانم احمدی بگویم که رضا کار نکرده.
lines.r: bāshad, vali ru-yam nemi-shavad be khānom-e Ahmadi beguyam ke Rezā kār na-karde.
lines.en: All right, but I'm too embarrassed to tell Ms Ahmadi that Reza hasn't done the work.
lines.col: باشه، ولی روم نمی‌شه به خانم احمدی بگم رضا کار نکرده.
lines.colR: bāshe, vali ru-m nemi-she be khānom-e Ahmadi begam Rezā kār na-karde.

lines.fa: لازم نیست. زبان به دهان بگیر؛ خودش دستش رو می‌شود.
lines.r: lāzem nist. zabān be dahān begir; khod-ash dast-ash ru mi-shavad.
lines.en: No need. Keep quiet – his game will be up on its own.
lines.col: لازم نیست. زبون به دهن بگیر؛ خودش دستش رو می‌شه.
lines.colR: lāzem nist. zabun be dahan begir; khod-ash dast-ash ru mi-she.

lines.fa: تو هم همیشه سر به سر من می‌گذاری! جدی می‌گویی؟
lines.r: to ham hamishe sar be sar-e man mi-gozāri! jeddi mi-guyi?
lines.en: You're always teasing me! Are you serious?
lines.col: تو هم همیشه سر به سر من می‌ذاری! جدی می‌گی؟
lines.colR: to ham hamishe sar be sar-e man mi-zāri! jeddi mi-gi?

lines.fa: این بار جدی‌ام. خانم احمدی گوشش از این حرف‌ها پر است.
lines.r: in bār jeddi-am. khānom-e Ahmadi gush-ash az in harf-hā por ast.
lines.en: This time I'm serious. Ms Ahmadi has heard it all before.
lines.col: این دفعه جدی‌ام. خانم احمدی گوشش از این حرفا پره.
lines.colR: in daf'e jeddi-am. khānom-e Ahmadi gush-ash az in harf-ā pore.
lines.lit: her ear is full of these words

lines.fa: باشد. پس امشب پا به پای هم کار می‌کنیم.
lines.r: bāshad. pas emshab pā be pā-ye ham kār mi-konim.
lines.en: OK. Then tonight we work side by side.
lines.col: باشه. پس امشب پا به پای هم کار می‌کنیم.
lines.colR: bāshe. pas emshab pā be pā-ye ham kār mi-konim.

lines.fa: و گوش به زنگ باش؛ اگر رضا زنگ زد، دلت به حالش نسوزد!
lines.r: o gush be zang bāsh; agar Rezā zang zad, del-at be hāl-ash na-suzad!
lines.en: And be on the alert – if Reza calls, don't go feeling sorry for him!
lines.col: گوش به زنگ باش؛ اگه رضا زنگ زد، دلت به حالش نسوزه!
lines.colR: gush be zang bāsh; age Rezā zang zad, del-at be hāl-ash na-suze!

lines.fa: قول نمی‌دهم. من دلم نازک است!
lines.r: ghowl nemi-daham. man del-am nāzok ast!

sections.title: Politeness lives in the body too
sections.md:
Many of the polite formulas you learned in A1 are body idioms in disguise. [[دستت درد نکند|dast-at dard na-konad|thank you]] wishes that the hand that worked for you may not hurt; the answer [[سرت درد نکند|sar-at dard na-konad]] wishes the same for your head. [[چشم|cheshm|yes, of course]] means 'on my eye' – I will do it as willingly as I would protect my own eyes – and a guest is told [[قدمتان روی چشم|ghadam-etān ru-ye cheshm|you are most welcome]], 'your step is on my eye'.

At a funeral or when someone has lost a relative, Iranians say [[سرتان سلامت باشد|sar-etān salāmat bāshad|my condolences]] – 'may your head be safe' – and the mourner answers [[سر شما هم سلامت باشد|sar-e shomā ham salāmat bāshad]]. You will also hear [[چشمت روشن|cheshm-at roshan]] at the other end of life, when a baby is born or a traveller comes home.

The liver deserves a word. In classical poetry lovers and mystics drink [[خون جگر|khun-e jegar|the blood of the liver]] – their suffering – and [[جگرسوز|jegar-suz|liver-burning]] describes anything heart-rending. So when a modern Iranian says that their liver has turned to kebab, they are speaking a very old language of feeling.

sections.title: Tips
items: Put the ending on the body part, not on the verb: دلم تنگ شده (I miss…), دلت تنگ شده (you miss…), never *دل تنگ شده‌ام.
Don't translate body idioms word for word into English – or English ones into Persian. 'To pull someone's leg' is سر به سر کسی گذاشتن, not پای کسی را کشیدن, which sounds bizarre.

Watch the register. سر کسی کلاه گذاشتن and دست از سرم بردار are fine with friends but too blunt for a formal letter; there you would write فریب دادن 'to deceive' or مزاحم نشوید 'please do not disturb'.
When you have said something a hundred times and nobody listens, Iranians say [[زبانم مو درآورد|zabān-am mu dar-āvard|I'm blue in the face]] – literally 'my tongue grew hair'.
A proverb to go with this lesson: [[زبان سرخ سر سبز می‌دهد بر باد|zabān-e sorkh sar-e sabz mi-dahad bar bād]] – 'the red tongue gives the green head to the wind': careless talk can cost you dearly.
Learn idioms in little scenes, not lists: imagine the hat being put on someone's head, the eye that refuses to drink, the liver on a skewer. The sillier the picture, the better you will remember it.

items.fa: وقتی عکس آن بچه را دیدم، جگرم ___ شد.
items.r: vaghti aks-e ān bacche rā didam, jegar-am ___ shod.
items.en: When I saw the photo of that child, my heart bled.

items.fa: زیادی به او ___ دادی؛ حالا هر کاری دلش می‌خواهد می‌کند.
items.r: ziyādi be u ___ dādi; hālā har kār-i del-ash mi-khāhad mi-konad.
items.en: You gave him too much leeway; now he does whatever he likes.

items.fa: شوخی کردم؛ داشتم سر به ___ می‌گذاشتم.
items.r: shukhi kardam; dāshtam sar be ___ mi-gozāshtam.
items.en: I was joking – I was just teasing you.

items.fa: منتظر خبرم و گوش به ___ هستم.
items.r: montazer-e khabar-am o gush be ___ hastam.
items.en: I'm waiting for news and on the alert.

items.explain: Literally 'my head is crowded' – too many things to think about.

items.q: A friend says [[فروشنده سرم کلاه گذاشت|forushande sar-am kolāh gozāsht]]. What happened?
options: The seller gave her a present
The seller sold her a hat
items.explain: 'To put a hat on someone's head' is to con them.

items.q: Your colleague's daughter has just had a baby. What do you say?
items.explain: چشمت روشن 'may your eyes be bright' is the congratulation for a birth or a return.
'My face can't manage it' – I'm too embarrassed to ask or say it.

items.q: Which idiom means 'to mediate between two people'?
items.explain: 'To put a foot in the middle' – to step in between people who have quarrelled.

items.q: What is the right way to say 'you miss him'?
items.explain: The ending goes on دل: دلت = your heart. دلم برایت تنگ شده would be 'I miss you'.

items.fa: دلمان خیلی برایت تنگ شده است.
items.r: del-emān kheyli barā-yat tang shode ast.

items.en: I'm too embarrassed to ask him.

items.fa: بیا دست به دست هم بدهیم.
items.r: biyā dast be dast-e ham bedahim.

items.fa: این هفته سرم خیلی شلوغ است.
items.r: in hafte sar-am kheyli sholugh ast.

items.fa: مهسا دلش را به دریا زد.
items.r: Mahsā del-ash rā be daryā zad.

items.fa: همه چشم به راه تو هستیم.
items.r: hame cheshm be rāh-e to hastim.
items.en: We are all waiting for you.

items.fa: چشمم آب نمی‌خورد که باران بیاید.
items.r: cheshm-am āb nemi-khorad ke bārān biyāyad.

items.fa: دلم برای کوچه‌های تهران تنگ شده است.
items.r: del-am barā-ye kuche-hā-ye Tehrān tang shode ast.
items.en: I miss the streets of Tehran.
options: I miss the streets of Tehran.
The streets of Tehran are narrow.
